content: A person's risk for developing AUD depends, in part, on how much, how often, and how quickly they consume alcohol. Alcohol misuse, which includes binge drinking and heavy alcohol use, over time increases the risk of AUD. Other factors also increase the risk of AUD, such as:

name: Drinking at an early age
content: Starting to drink at a young age is associated with a higher likelihood of developing alcohol use disorder later in life. Early alcohol exposure can affect the developing brain and increase the chances of heavier or more frequent use over time. Research suggests that delaying the age of first drink is one of the most consistent protective factors.

name: Genetics and family history of alcohol problems
content: Genetics play a role, with heritability approximately 60 percent; however, like other chronic health conditions, AUD risk is influenced by the interplay between a person's genes and their environment. Parents' drinking patterns may also influence the likelihood that a child will one day develop AUD.

name: Mental health conditions and a history of trauma
content: A wide range of psychiatric conditions—including depression, post-traumatic stress disorder, and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder—are comorbid with AUD and are associated with an increased risk of AUD. People with a history of childhood trauma are also vulnerable to AUD.
